newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: SWIMMING-SMITH MAKES TRIUMPHANT RETURN TO IRELAND.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-SMITH MAKES TRIUMPHANT RETURN TO IRELAND.

text.p: Swimming in Ireland for the first time since her Olympic triumphs in Atlanta, Michelle Smith delighted her supporters with a national record on Sunday but declined to discuss the sensitive issue of drug-testing.
Smith became a sporting heroine in Ireland after winning three gold medals at the 1996 Atlanta Games in an astonishing advance at the late swimming age of 26.

She was given a rousing reception when she arrived on the poolside for the final of the 200 metres freestyle in Galway and received a standing ovation from some of the crowd after setting a national short-course record of two minutes 1.38 seconds.

Smith, who won gold medals in the 200 and 400 metres individual medley and 400 freestyle and a bronze in the 200 butterfly in Atlanta, smiled and looked relaxed as she signed programmes and T-shirts for young autograph hunters.
The same carnival atmosphere had prevailed when Smith won the 100 metres individual medley on Saturday.

On both days hundreds of spectators had been left outside the venue ticketless. Tickets had sold out in a day and fans who could not get in had to be content with watching the swimming on a big screen set up nearby.
But the smiles on Smith's face disappeared when journalists tried to ask her questions about drug testing.
"I would like to restrict questions to my swimming this weekend if that's okay. Any other questions can be dealt with through my solicitor," Smith said.

Smith's extraordinary progress after finishing among the also-rans at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics provoked tough questions for the swimmer in Atlanta. She categorically denied ever using performance-enhancing drugs.
Smith underwent a dope test on Saturday, the first carried out by the Irish Amateur Swimming Association (IASA) on a swimmer competing in Ireland.
The results of the test will be sent to swimming's world governing body, the International Amateur Swimming Federation (FINA).
FINA confirmed last month that Smith failed to appear for an out-of-competition doping test at her home in County Kildare last October.
She was attending a public function in her honour in New York on that date and did not return home until two days later.

FINA executive director Cornel Marculescu said last month: "The rules say if you have two no-shows you may face sanctions...She has not violated any FINA rules. She had one no-show but this is normal, it happens to many, many swimmers. She has been tested at least once since then. We've had no problems with her."

Smith was guarded at the weekend about her future competition plans, saying she would decide whether or not to take part in August's European championships in Seville and next January's world championships in Perth, Australia, nearer the time. "I don't make decisions in advance," she said.
Smith has made enormous strides since she teamed up with Dutch discus thrower Erik de Bruin after the 1992 Barcelona Olympics.

De Bruin, a former world silver medallist who is serving a four-year ban from athletics for doping, made major changes to her training, bringing in techniques from athletics. The couple are now married.

Smith made her international breakthrough in the 1995 World Cup short-course series and went on claim two golds and a silver at the 1995 European long-course championships in Vienna, a year before her Atlanta triumphs.
